sources.title: Charlotte Wickham, Statistics: Lecture Three — Linear Models
sources.locator: PDF pp. 2–3: §1 The Theory, response and predictor measurement layout, Matrix Representation, Example - Simple Regression, and Example - Analysis of Variance.

contents.name: The Theory: response and predictor measurement layout
contents.support: The contract defines measurable response and predictor maps and requires the observation and unit roles to be declared; it imports no linear-model likelihood or inference claim.

contents.name: Matrix Representation
contents.reason: The matrix equation Y=Xβ+ε and least-squares model details belong to the later fixed-design regression pair, not the general model-contract definition.

contents.name: Example - Simple Regression
contents.reason: This simple-regression model and its error assumptions are reserved for the fixed-design regression pair; the present pair records model fields only.

contents.name: Example - Analysis of Variance
contents.reason: The grouped response illustration is recognized as a linear-model special case, but its ANOVA model and inferential results are assigned to the fixed-design regression development.

sources.title: Fan Li, STA610 Lecture 1 Notes: The Problem of Correlated Data
sources.locator: PDF pp. 1–4: §§1.1–1.4 and §§2.1–2.3, including the page-1 contents headings used to identify these sections.

contents.name: 1.1 The model in scalar and matrix form
contents.support: The contract requires a declared response, predictor, observation record, and probability law while keeping model assumptions explicit.

contents.name: 1.2 The Gauss–Markov assumptions
contents.reason: These are model-specific regression hypotheses; the contract requires authors to list such assumptions but proves no Gauss–Markov or regression result.

contents.name: 1.3 The OLS estimator and why it is unbiased regardless of assumption 4
contents.reason: The conditional unbiasedness calculation is an estimator theorem assigned to the fixed-design regression pair, not to the definition of a scientific model contract.

contents.name: 1.4 The variance of the OLS estimator
contents.reason: The OLS covariance formula and BLUE conclusion require their own fixed-design hypotheses and proof in the later regression pair.

contents.name: Key takeaway on mean and variance assumptions
contents.reason: The distinction between unbiasedness, efficiency, and standard-error validity is specific regression theory and is not asserted by this bookkeeping definition.

contents.name: 2.1 Notation for nested data
contents.support: The example separately indexes participant, visit, and technical-readout units and does not infer independence from their nested layout.

contents.name: Running example
contents.support: The example uses a different scientific setting but retains the source's structural distinction between a cluster-level assignment unit and lower-level repeated observations.

contents.name: 2.2 The question: what happens if we ignore the clustering and just run OLS?
contents.reason: The effect of clustering on OLS inference is a mixed-model and covariance result; this example addresses units and design bookkeeping without claiming an inferential consequence.

contents.name: 2.3 Building the two-component (random-intercept) model from first principles
contents.reason: The random-intercept law and its covariance consequences are assigned to the mixed-effects pair; they are not imported into this unit-indexing example.
